Nimbus is a private, non-commercial weather app. Data: Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD) via Open-Meteo and Bright Sky, ECMWF, Météo-France and other national weather services via Open-Meteo, CAMS air quality, RainViewer, Sensor.Community. Maps © OpenFreeMap, OpenMapTiles, OpenStreetMap contributors.

The moon orbits the Earth in about 29.5 days. Depending on its position relative to the sun we see a different part of its sunlit half:
• New moon: the moon is between Earth and sun and invisible
• Waxing: the lit part grows, in the evening sky
• Full moon: opposite the sun, rises at sunset
• Waning: the lit part shrinks, visible in the second half of the night and in the morning

Moonrise and moonset shift by roughly 50 minutes each day, so on some days the moon does not rise or set at all.

The app calculates phase, illumination and rise/set times astronomically on the device (after J. Meeus and SunCalc) – no data source is needed. At night the animated sky shows the moon in its real phase when it is above the horizon.

The next 24 hours at a glance. The symbol shows the most likely weather for the hour, the number below it the temperature.

• Now: the current weather – where available measured at the nearest DWD station, therefore it can differ slightly from the forecast for this hour
• Percentages: chance of precipitation – blue from 10 %, below that dimmed – see the precipitation card for details
• Sun symbols with a time: sunrise and sunset

The sentence above summarises the next change in weather and strong gusts. Swipe sideways for more hours.

One row per day: symbol, lowest and highest temperature.

• The bar shows the day's temperature range on a scale common to all ten days – so warmer and colder days are easy to compare
• Its colours go from blue (cold) via green and yellow to red (hot)
• The dot on today's bar is the current temperature
• Blue percentages: chance of precipitation on that day

Tap a day to see its temperature curve and hourly precipitation. Days 9 and 10 have larger uncertainty.

A short text forecast for the next 12 hours, generated automatically from the hourly forecast of the selected weather model (default: DWD ICON). It is not written by a meteorologist.

It names the next change in weather, how the temperature develops, whether and when precipitation is likely (from 60 %) or possible (from 30 %), strong gusts from 50 km/h and – in the afternoon and evening – a short outlook for tomorrow.

If it is raining now, the end of the precipitation comes from the 15-minute forecast.
No DWD station nearby – forecast values only (%1$s)

Swipe right from the current weather to see today so far, yesterday and the day before.

In Germany the values are measurements of the nearest DWD weather station (via Bright Sky). Next to them the app shows what the selected weather model had forecast for the same hours – so you can see how good the forecast was. The mean deviation is the average difference between forecast and measured temperature, hour by hour.

Outside Germany, or without a station nearby, only the model values are available.

The data is loaded when you swipe and not stored permanently; it is always the current state of the sources.
No precipitation in the forecast values.

The percentage shows how likely it is that at least a small, measurable amount of precipitation (about 0.1 mm) falls at your location within that hour or day.

30% does not mean that it rains 30% of the time or over 30% of the area. It means: in 3 out of 10 comparable weather situations it rains at this place. The value is derived from ensemble forecasts – many slightly varied model runs – and counts how many of them produce rain.

The symbol still shows the most likely weather – so a cloud with 40 % means: probably dry, but a real chance of a shower. Values below 10 % are shown dimmed.

The feels-like (apparent) temperature describes how warm or cold it feels to the human body, not what a thermometer measures in the shade.

Wind removes body heat faster, so it feels colder than the air temperature (wind chill). High humidity hinders sweat from evaporating, so warm air feels even warmer. Strong sunshine can also make it feel warmer.

When the current temperature is measured at a DWD station, the feels-like value is shifted by the same difference.

Relative humidity is how much water vapour the air holds compared to the maximum it could hold at its current temperature. Because warm air can hold more water, the same amount of moisture gives a lower percentage in the afternoon than at night.

The dew point is the temperature to which the air would have to cool down for water vapour to condense – for dew, fog or condensation on windows. It describes the actual moisture content better than relative humidity:
• below 10°: dry and pleasant
• 10–⁠16°: comfortable
• 16–⁠20°: noticeably humid
• above 20°: muggy and oppressive

If temperature and dew point are close together, fog or low clouds are likely.

The UV index measures the strength of the sun's ultraviolet radiation, which causes sunburn and skin damage. It depends on the sun's height, clouds, ozone and altitude.

• 0–⁠2 low: no protection needed
• 3–⁠5 moderate: protection recommended around midday
• 6–⁠7 high: protection required, seek shade at midday
• 8–⁠10 very high: avoid the sun at midday
• 11+ extreme

Snow, water and sand reflect UV radiation and increase exposure. Clouds reduce it, but thin clouds let most UV through.

Wind speed is the average over about 10 minutes, measured at a height of 10 m. Gusts are short peaks lasting a few seconds and can be much stronger than the average.

The direction is where the wind comes from: a west wind blows from west to east. The arrow in the compass points where the wind is blowing to.

Beaufort scale (examples): 3 = gentle breeze (12–⁠19 km/h), 5 = fresh breeze (29–⁠38), 7 = near gale (50–⁠61), 9 = strong gale (75–⁠88), 12 = hurricane force (≥ 118 km/h). The animated background shows wind and gusts too – clouds, rain and leaves move with them.

Visibility is the distance at which objects can still be clearly recognised. It is reduced by fog, mist, haze, precipitation, dust or smoke.

Meteorologists speak of fog when visibility is below 1 km. Values above 20 km mean very clear air. Visibility is measured automatically at DWD stations; otherwise it comes from the forecast model.

High humidity and good visibility are not a contradiction: water vapour itself is invisible. Visibility only drops when it condenses into tiny droplets (mist, fog – usually above about 95 %) or when dust and soot particles swell up in moist air (haze). After rain has washed the air clean, 40 km at 80–90 % humidity is quite normal.

Air pressure is the weight of the air column above us, given in hectopascals (hPa) and reduced to sea level so values from different altitudes can be compared. The average is about 1013 hPa.

High pressure (above ~1020 hPa) usually brings calm, dry weather. Low pressure (below ~1000 hPa) often brings clouds, wind and precipitation.

The trend matters more than the value: rapidly falling pressure indicates an approaching low and deteriorating weather, rising pressure indicates improvement. The arrow shows the change over the next three hours.

The European Air Quality Index (EAQI) of the European Environment Agency combines fine dust (PM2.5, PM10), nitrogen dioxide, ozone and sulphur dioxide into one number. The worst pollutant determines the index.

• 0–⁠20 good • 20–⁠40 fair • 40–⁠60 moderate • 60–⁠80 poor • 80–⁠100 very poor • above 100 extremely poor

PM2.5 and PM10 are particles smaller than 2.5 and 10 micrometres; the smaller ones reach deep into the lungs. The values come from the Copernicus CAMS model for Europe.

The pollen forecast shows how strongly allergy-relevant pollen types are in the air.

Levels (scale of the German Weather Service): none, low, moderate and high, with intermediate steps. Each bar has three segments – half-filled segments are the intermediate steps.

• Germany: official DWD pollen forecast for 8 types (hazel, alder, ash, birch, grasses, rye, mugwort, ragweed) and 27 regions, issued daily around 11:00 for today, tomorrow and the day after
• Rest of Europe: levels derived from the Copernicus CAMS model (6 types)

Composition and course come from CAMS in grains per cubic metre of air. They show which pollen dominates – useful if you react to only some types. Sensitive people can react even at low levels.

When pollen is in the air and it is dry, the animated background shows it as fine floating particles.

This short-range forecast shows expected precipitation in 15-minute steps. In Germany it comes from the DWD\'s high-resolution ICON-D2 model (2.2 km grid), which is updated every three hours.\n\nThe bars show the amount per 15 minutes. For the current rain radar, including the DWD radar nowcast for the next two hours, open the precipitation map.

Weather radar sends out microwave pulses and measures how strongly raindrops, snowflakes and hail reflect them (reflectivity in dBZ). Stronger echoes mean heavier precipitation.

Germany: DWD radar composite in 5-minute steps plus a nowcast that extrapolates the movement of the precipitation for the next two hours. Rest of Europe: RainViewer (past two hours only).

Both sources are shown in one colour scale. Radar sees precipitation in the air: light drizzle or snow close to the ground may be missing, and near mountains or radar sites artefacts can occur.

Weather models are computer simulations that calculate the future state of the atmosphere on a three-dimensional grid. Finer grids resolve local effects such as thunderstorms, valleys and coasts better.

• ICON-D2 (DWD): 2.2 km, Germany & neighbours, 2 days
• ICON-EU (DWD): 7 km, Europe, 5 days
• ECMWF IFS: 9–⁠25 km, global, one of the best global models
• AROME/ARPEGE (Météo-France), UK Met Office, KNMI Harmonie, MET Norway, NOAA GFS

If the lines lie close together, the forecast is fairly certain. If they diverge, the weather situation is uncertain – typical for thunderstorms or several days ahead. Tap a model to highlight it.

Sensor.Community is an open network of thousands of self-built sensors run by citizens – similar to OpenStreetMap, but for measurements. The data is freely available.

Private sensors are not calibrated and are often mounted on balconies or house walls, sometimes in the sun. The app therefore shows the median of all outdoor sensors nearby and removes outliers. The spread shows how much the sensors disagree.

Use these values as an additional local impression; the official DWD station is more reliable.

Near a DWD weather station the current values (temperature, humidity, wind, pressure, visibility) are real measurements from the nearest station within 30 km, provided by Bright Sky from DWD open data. Otherwise they come from the forecast model for the exact location.\n\nMeasurements are more accurate for the station itself, but local conditions can differ – for example between a city centre and an airport. You can switch this off in the settings.

Official warnings of the Deutscher Wetterdienst for your municipality, colour-coded by severity:

• Yellow – weather warning: possible hazard, e.g. frost, strong gusts
• Orange – warning of significant weather: dangerous weather, e.g. storm gusts, heavy rain
• Red – severe weather warning: very dangerous, e.g. hurricane-force gusts, heavy thunderstorms
• Purple – extreme severe weather warning: extremely dangerous, take protective measures

Warnings are only available for Germany.
